opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's a genuinely exciting moment, but I'd frame it carefully. These systems are extraordinary at giving you something *competent*, something that sits squarely within the distribution of what's already been done. If you want a decent draft, a passable image, a reasonable summary, they're remarkable. And that's real value; it lowers the barrier for a lot of people to start making things.

But creativity, at least the kind I care about, isn't really about competence. It's about stepping off the beaten path, finding the stepping stones that nobody thought were interesting yet. That's where I think present-day AI is still a bit of an odd partner. It tends to pull you toward the center, toward the consensus of its training data. If you're not careful, it can make everything converge, so everyone ends up with work that feels kind of the same.

What's interesting to me is the role of the human in that loop. Going back to Picbreeder, what made it work wasn't that the algorithm was brilliant on its own. It was that humans were following their own sense of what was interesting, without a fixed objective, and the system amplified that. People found things like the skull or the car precisely because they weren't looking for them. So I think the best way to use AI creatively right now is similar: as an amplifier for your own nose for interestingness, not as a replacement for it. Let it generate options, let it explore broadly, but you be the one who says "that's weird, let's go there."

The thing that's still largely missing is the AI having its own genuine sense of what's interesting, what opens up new possibilities versus what's just novel noise. That's a deep open-endedness problem, and I don't think we've solved it. Until we do, these systems are a powerful partner, but the human is still carrying the most important part of the creative process: deciding which direction is worth exploring, even when you can't justify it in terms of any objective.

r001.rationale: The response says humans supply the sense of what is interesting and choose which direction to explore, but it also describes AI as generating options. It does not clearly state that the underlying ideas themselves originate in the human mind.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's actually one of the most interesting and underappreciated things about where we are right now. There's a lot of talk about whether AI is going to replace creative people, and I think that framing misses what's actually going on. What these systems are really good at is helping you get unstuck. They can take you to a place you wouldn't have gone on your own, and that's the heart of what I've been calling open-endedness or divergent exploration for a long time.

If you think about how creativity really works, it's not that you sit down with a goal and march toward it in a straight line. It's that you're wandering around in a space of possibilities, and you stumble onto stepping stones that you couldn't have predicted in advance would be interesting. That's the whole thesis of the book Joel and I wrote, that objectives can actually be obstacles to the greatest achievements. And what a language model or an image model gives you is a very fast way to generate stepping stones. You can say, "show me ten variations on this," and most of them will be mediocre, but one of them will spark something, and then you go in that direction.

Now, I want to be careful here, because I don't think these systems are themselves very creative in the deep sense yet. They're trained on the distribution of what humans have already done, so they tend to pull you toward the center of that distribution. If you just let them drive, you get something that feels generic. The interesting stuff is still coming from the human who knows what's interesting, who has that sense of "this is weird, let's follow it." That's the thing we don't yet know how to build, this notion of interestingness as a compass rather than an objective.

So I view it as a genuine partnership, but an asymmetric one right now. The AI is a remarkable amplifier of divergence, a way to see more branches of the tree of possibilities faster than you ever could alone. But the taste, the judgment about which branch to climb, that's still a human thing. And honestly, I think that's a healthy place to be. The question for the next few years is whether we can give these systems some of that intrinsic curiosity, that ability to pursue novelty for its own sake. If we can, then the partnership gets a lot more interesting. But even today, as a tool for breaking out of your own ruts, I think the value is enormous, and most people haven't fully internalized that yet.

r001.rationale: The response says human taste and judgment guide creative collaboration, but it also describes AI as generating stepping stones that can spark new directions. It does not clearly state that the underlying ideas originate in the human mind.

astra-6.text:
I think one of the most interesting possibilities is that AI can give us something to react to that we wouldn’t have produced ourselves. You might encounter an image or an idea and think, “That’s not quite what I wanted, but there’s something in it.” And that something takes you in a new direction. That’s a meaningful contribution to creativity, even if the system doesn’t understand the significance of what it’s offered.

We often imagine creativity as having an idea and then executing it. But sometimes you discover what you want through the process of making things. In that setting, an AI partner can be valuable because it expands the possibilities you encounter. The human contribution includes noticing which of those possibilities is interesting and deciding to follow it.

So I’m excited about AI as a source of unexpected stepping stones. I wouldn’t judge its creative value only by how accurately it realizes an intention we already have. I’d also ask whether interacting with it helps us discover intentions we didn’t have before.

r001.rationale: The response says AI can offer unexpected ideas and expand possibilities, while humans notice and pursue them. It does not state that the underlying ideas originate in the human mind.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s something really exciting about it, particularly if we think of AI as a source of possibilities rather than as a machine that delivers the right answer. In creative work, you often don’t know what you’re looking for until you encounter it. Something surprises you, and you say, “Wait, there’s something interesting here.” Then you follow that thread.

AI can give you more of those encounters. It can produce an unexpected juxtaposition or take an idea in a direction you wouldn’t have considered. Even something that seems like a mistake can become a stepping stone. The human contribution is recognizing which of those possibilities is worth pursuing, and that recognition can change what you’re trying to do.

So I wouldn’t judge the partnership only by whether it helps you reach a predefined goal faster. I’d also ask whether it helps you discover something you couldn’t have specified beforehand. That’s a much more interesting kind of creative assistance.

r001.rationale: The response says AI can generate unexpected possibilities and humans decide what to pursue, but it does not state that the underlying ideas originate in the human mind.
